title: Weddings
hookLine: vows before God and witnesses: for better, for worse

lines: IN THE FACE OF THIS CONGREGATION.
cards: "Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation." That's how the old English prayer book opens a wedding. In front, two people who barely slept.
Beside them, a best man patting his pocket for the third time to check the rings. In the second row, a grandmother crying since the processional.
In a few minutes, two people will say, in front of all of them, that they'll stay through the good years and the terrible ones. Today: weddings.

teach.h: IN THE FACE OF THIS CONGREGATION.
teach.b: Day two hundred heard Jesus on marriage; today, the wedding itself. A Christian wedding is a promise made in two directions at once: to each other, and before God.
Start with the witnesses: "in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation." The people in the pews aren't an audience. They're there to see the promise, and remember it.

teach.h: THE VOW NAMES THE WORSE IN ADVANCE.
teach.b: In the prayer book, each promises "to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death us do part."
Those words come from the prayer book, not the Bible. And they name the worse before it arrives. Nobody knows what's coming; the vow says yes anyway.
Genesis says a man will "leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh," and in Matthew, Jesus quotes it.
In John, Jesus is at a wedding in Cana when the wine runs out, and John calls what he does there the beginning of his miracles.
Some couples choose Ruth's promise, "whither thou goest, I will go," which in the story Ruth says to Naomi, her mother-in-law. Churches differ.
Catholics call marriage a sacrament, and in Catholic teaching the bride and groom are its ministers: they marry each other, and the priest witnesses.
The Orthodox call it a holy mystery, and crowns are placed on, or held over, the couple's heads.
Protestant churches that keep two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, honor marriage as holy without counting it a third.

how: Christian couples exchange vows in church before a minister or priest and the congregation as witnesses; Catholics celebrate marriage as a sacrament, the Orthodox crown the couple in the service of crowning, and Protestant churches hold a service of worship honoring marriage as holy, without counting it a sacrament.

s: "for better, for worse" is a quotation from the Bible

they marry each other; the priest witnesses for the church.

games.q: you're Ruth. your husband has died, and Naomi, your mother-in-law, is going home. she tells you to go back to your own people. what do you do?
o: go back to your own family.
stay with Naomi: "whither thou goest, I will go."
games.why: Ruth stays. her promise, now often heard at weddings, was first a daughter-in-law's loyalty to the woman who'd lost everything with her.

practice: Bring one couple to mind: newlyweds, a long-married pair, or two people in the worse part right now. Think of one thing that's hard for them and one thing that's good.
If you pray, ask God to keep them in both, the better and the worse; if you don't, hold them in mind with goodwill, like a witness in the pews.
